title: Counting & comparing
blurb: Bigger, smaller, and the friends that make ten.

gator.name: Bigger or smaller
gator.phrase: The hungry alligator eats the bigger number.
gator.also: The pointy end points at the smaller number.
steps: The alligator’s open mouth faces the bigger one.
The point faces the smaller one.
gator.exception: If both numbers are the same, there is nothing bigger to eat. Use = instead. The mouth faces the bigger number, not whichever number comes first.

bonds.name: Friends of ten
bonds.phrase: Ten friends hold hands: 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, 5 and 5.
steps: Fill the ten frame with the first number.
The empty boxes are the partner.
bonds.exception: These partners only make 10. For 20, the partners change: 7 needs 13. And 0’s partner is the whole 10.

counton.name: Counting on
counton.phrase: Put the big number in your head, then count on.
steps: Count up one finger for each of the smaller number.
The last number you say is the answer.
counton.exception: Do not start again from 1. And do not count the starting number twice: 8 + 3 is 9, 10, 11, not 8, 9, 10.

maketen.name: Make a ten
maketen.phrase: Make a ten, then add the rest.
maketen.also: 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3. The 2 fills the ten, and the 3 is the rest.
steps: Take just enough from the other number to make 10.
maketen.exception: Take only what fills the ten: for 8 + 5, take 2, not 5. If the total is less than 10, there is no ten to make, so just count on.

teens.name: Teen numbers
teens.phrase: A teen is ten and some more.
teens.also: Fourteen is ten and four. The 1 in front is the ten.
steps: The 1 in front stands for one ten.
The last digit tells how many more.
teens.exception: Eleven and twelve don’t say “teen”, but they are ten and 1, and ten and 2. Fourteen is written 14, not 41, and not 104.

neardbl.name: Doubles and near doubles
neardbl.phrase: Doubles plus one: double the small number, then add one more.
steps: A double is the same number twice: 6 + 6 = 12.
For a near double, double the smaller number.
neardbl.exception: Double the smaller number, then add 1. If you double the bigger one, take 1 away instead: 6 + 7 is 14 − 1. It only works for next-door numbers: 6 + 8 is double 6 plus 2.

skip.name: Counting by 2s, 5s, and 10s
skip.also: Fives end in 5 or 0. Tens always end in 0.
steps: By 10s: the tens digit goes up by 1, and the ones digit stays 0.
skip.exception: Keep the jump the same every time. Counting by 10s from 20 goes 20, 30, 40, not 20, 21, 22. If you start on an odd number, counting by 2s gives odd numbers: 3, 5, 7.

allword.name: Word clues: all / altogether
allword.phrase: All, altogether, in all, total — those words mean add.
allword.also: How many in all? Put the parts together.
steps: Find the clue word: all, altogether, in all, total, sum.
allword.exception: “All” with “left” or “gone” can mean subtract. Read the whole sentence.

leftword.name: Word clues: left / remain
leftword.phrase: Left, remain, take away, how many more — those words mean subtract.
steps: Find the clue: left, remain, take away, how many more, difference.
leftword.exception: “How many more” compares two amounts: bigger − smaller. Start with the whole, not the leftover.

eachword.name: Word clues: each / groups
eachword.phrase: Each, every, groups of — those words often mean multiply (or equal shares).
eachword.also: 3 bags with 4 each: three groups of four.
eachword.exception: “Each” can also mean divide when you share: 12 stickers, 3 each means how many kids?

shareword.name: Word clues: share / split
shareword.phrase: Share equally, split, divide among — those words mean divide.
steps: Find how many in each group (or how many groups).
shareword.exception: Sharing must be fair. Leftovers are a remainder — don’t pretend they vanish.

commute.name: Order of addends
commute.phrase: You can flip the addends: 3 + 5 is the same as 5 + 3.
commute.also: Commutative: the commute is the same both ways.
steps: Start with the bigger number in your head.
commute.exception: Order does not matter for + and ×. It does matter for − and ÷: 5 − 3 is not 3 − 5.

countback.name: Counting back
countback.phrase: Put the big number in your head, then count back.
steps: Count back one finger for each you take away.
The last number you say is the answer.
countback.exception: Do not count the starting number as a finger. 9 − 2 is 8, 7 — not 9, 8.

zeroadd.name: Adding zero
zeroadd.phrase: Zero is the do-nothing number for adding.
zeroadd.also: Plus zero keeps the number the same.
steps: The other number stays the same.
zeroadd.exception: Zero is special for + and × differently: n + 0 = n, but n × 0 = 0.

estimate.name: About how many?
estimate.phrase: Estimate: is it closer to a friendly ten?
steps: 5 or more → bump up to the next ten.
4 or less → stay at this ten.
estimate.exception: Estimating is a “about” answer, not exact. Use it to check if an exact answer looks wild.

morefewer.name: More and fewer
morefewer.phrase: More means bigger. Fewer means smaller.
morefewer.exception: Fewer is for things you can count. For continuous stuff people say “less,” but the compare idea is the same.

partwhole.name: Part–part–whole
partwhole.phrase: Two parts make the whole. The whole splits into parts.
steps: Parts add to the whole; whole minus a part leaves the other part.
partwhole.exception: Don’t mix which number is the whole. The whole is always the total, never a leftover part.

tenmore.name: Ten more, ten less
tenmore.phrase: Ten more bumps the tens digit up. Ten less bumps it down.
steps: Ten more: add 1 to the tens.
Ten less: subtract 1 from the tens.
tenmore.exception: Ones stay put when you add or subtract exactly 10. 27 + 10 is 37, not 28.

sameboth.name: Same on both sides
sameboth.phrase: If both sides match, use the equals sign.
sameboth.also: Balance: what you do to one side, keep the story true.
steps: If not, they are not equal.
sameboth.exception: Equals means “same value,” not “looks the same.” 3 + 5 and 4 + 4 both equal 8.

fingeradd.name: Fingers for small sums
fingeradd.phrase: Hold the bigger number; raise fingers for the smaller; count them on.
steps: Put the bigger number in your head (or on one hand).
Raise one finger for each of the smaller number.
Count on from the big number.
fingeradd.exception: When the sum goes past 10, make a ten first, then use the leftover fingers.

beforeafter.name: Before and after
beforeafter.phrase: Before is one less. After is one more.
steps: The number line is your friend.
beforeafter.exception: Before 0 you leave the everyday counting numbers — kindergarten stays at 0 and up.

howmany.name: How many more?
howmany.phrase: How many more? Start at the smaller, count up to the bigger.
howmany.exception: “How many more” is a compare, not a take-away story with leftovers on a plate.

dblfacts.name: Doubles facts
dblfacts.phrase: A double is the same number twice: 6 + 6 = 12.
steps: Double means add the number to itself.
dblfacts.exception: Near doubles are next door (6 + 7). Pure doubles are exact twins.
